questions.problem: Which of the following is the graph of $y=-2({3}^{x})+1?$
questions.worked_solution:
To plot the given function, we follow these steps:

- We take the curve $y=2({3}^{x}).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14216573/assets/7a11b33423337a8d7f0222e1586753d62374f3d8b3eca02cccadd99e50b9eb1b.png)

- Reflect it on the $x$-axis to give $y=-2({3}^{x}).$ The $y$-intercept moves from $(0,2)$ to $(0,-2)$ but the horizontal asymptote stays at $y=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14216573/assets/53aedebd12a8f1138efcc9e9815dba7cf15d869da4f321274f6b0cd367e28cac.png)

- Then, vertically shift it by $1$ unit up to give $y=-2({3}^{x})+1.$ The point $(0,-2)$ moves to $(0,-1)$ and the horizontal asymptote moves from $y=0$ to $y=1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14216573/assets/d862abef96431d8165d0b6c1fd76419597f828824fab1bf88eb4ccba5e6dfda8.png)

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To plot the given function, we follow these steps:

- We take the curve $y=\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{x}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14216573/assets/e9331b26e26b99d3d8fcaea0bb7864b45f697211d3f30c41e9cc5329b1ef5d45.png)

- Reflect it on the $x$-axis to give $y=-\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{x}.$ The $y$-intercept moves from $(0,1)$ to $(0,-1)$ but the horizontal asymptote stays at $y=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14216573/assets/df29fef3da108d38afc6a0275cc8b0f52237915576a8d7528f90ffeab5588264.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14216573/assets/e63aa682e19fef317badd419805ffd82a449559a159a41650d2260daf33eff76.png)

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
To plot the graph of $y=-2(3^x),$ we take the curve $y=2(3^x)$ and reflect it in the $x$-axis, as shown below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14216573/assets/6130842f788070c7e97fe82698b701293af681a6aba3acfce0f4dde269cddbcf.png)

This transformation is called a **reflection in the $\boldsymbol{x}$-axis**, and it occurs because the output $y$-values of the function $y=2(3^x)$ are made negative by the transformation.

If we combine vertical translations with reflection, we get a general form

$$
y = -a(b^x) + k.
$$

This is the equation of a reflected exponential graph $y=-a(b^x)$ that is translated $k$ units up.
